newsitem.title: GERMANY: Doubts on Kohl rise in CDU amid tax reform turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Doubts on Kohl rise in CDU amid tax reform turmoil.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) were racked by internal turmoil on Sunday amid a bitter dispute over the government's controversial tax and pension reform plans.

Kohl chastised his labour minister and long-time party ally Norbert Bluem for his "completely unacceptable" public doubts about Kohl's word while CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble warned "poisonous" in-fighting was harming the party.

"We are destroying ourselves with this debate," Schaeuble said, referring to a row sparked by rare public criticism of Kohl from young up-and-coming CDU leaders over tax reform. "Personalising this will lead nowhere."
Kohl, who has masterfully beat back uprisings from within his party ranks during his 14-year reign as chancellor, told CDU leaders he was ready to tackle the latest rebellion.

"The people against me are there in the bushes again and now they think they might dare to come out into the open," Kohl said, according to a report in Der Spiegel news magazine to be published on Monday. It reminded him, Kohl said, of the last failed putsch in 1989.

But as editorials, opposition leaders and even some CDU officials were doubting Kohl had the ability, ideas and energy to lead the country out of its economic and financial malaise, the chancellor renewed a threat to quit, Der Spiegel said.
The CDU "should look for someone else" if Germany fails to reduce budget deficits enough to qualify for European Monetary Union (EMU), Kohl, 66, told the CDU presidium in January.
The chancellery had no immediate comment on the report.

Kohl wants to slash income tax and corporate tax rates while scrapping 70 tax breaks in measures that would leave taxpayers 30 billion marks ($18.3 billion) better off. But many CDU leaders oppose raising value-added tax to finance the cuts.

"Helmut Kohl has until now been the untouchable icon, party leader and federal chancellor -- but he is now being openly attacked," wrote the Hamburger Abendblatt in an editorial. "Kohl is standing in front of a pile of ruins."
The years without any criticism from within "are apparently over", a Kohl adviser told Der Spiegel. "A major change in the weather climate is upon us."

The chancellor's criticism of Bluem, a staunch ally who is one of the few in Bonn who addresses Kohl with the informal "Du", caused an immmediate stir because the departure of Bluem would expose a potentially-lethal rift in the government.
After admonishing Bluem, Kohl quickly said he had no intention of firing the popular labour minister.
Bluem had said in a newspaper interview that Kohl's promises could no longer be trusted and told parliament on Friday he would not hide his dispute with Kohl behind closed doors any longer.

Calling the doubts about his word "completely unacceptable", Kohl appeared stunned by the remark from Bluem, who has served in every Kohl cabinet since 1982. Kohl asked in an interview with Focus newsmagazine: "Did he really say that?"
The chancellor added: "We are good friends so we should also be able to have a dispute...Bluem is in the cabinet and I have absolutely no intention of changing that."
Bluem had been seething in private for weeks over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to raise taxes on pensions and over other matters linked to the sweeping tax reform proposals.
Bluem unveiled plans last week to cut old-age pensions, raise contributions and launch a tax-financed "family fund" to keep the compulsory pensions scheme going in the 21st century.
Even Kohl's coalition partners, the centrist Free Democrats (FDP), urged the CDU to put the dispute behind it.
"We are counting on the CDU to bring an end to their internal fight and return to our course of reform policies," said FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt on Sunday.
